entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To succeed in getting a job, especially a good one that took effort or beat strong competition.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, news and career advice, and it sounds like a success story after effort: *She landed a job at NASA*. The same verb works with *a contract, a deal, an interview, a role, a big client*. In a cover letter or formal report, *obtain* or *secure a position* sounds more formal.
entries.pattern: land a job (at / with + employer; as + role)
examples: After six months of applications, my cousin finally **landed a job** at a hospital in Boston.
Being bilingual helped him **land a job** with an airline right out of college.
Fewer recent graduates are **landing jobs** in their field than ten years ago.

drill.sentence: Remember the kid next door who could never sit still? He just {{landed a job}} as a stunt driver in Hollywood.
drill.hint: succeeded in getting hired (the verb is also used for planes touching down)

entries.related: *get a job* — plain and neutral; *secure a position* — formal, for writing; *score a job* — slangier, stresses luck.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A win that brings no real benefit or satisfaction, because the cost was too high or the prize turned out to mean little.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, sports and politics, and in personal stories about lawsuits, divorces or family fights. It usually follows *be*, *prove* or *feel like*, as in *It proved a hollow victory*. Compared with *a Pyrrhic victory*, which stresses heavy losses, *hollow* stresses the empty feeling afterward.
entries.pattern: be / prove / feel like a hollow victory
examples: We won the lawsuit, but after three years of legal fees, it was **a hollow victory**.
Beating a team that had rested all its starters felt like **a hollow victory**.
Critics called the bill's passage **a hollow victory**, since most of its key provisions had been stripped out.

drill.sentence: She finally got an apology from her ex, but by then she no longer cared, so it felt like {{a hollow victory}}.
drill.hint: a win that brought no real satisfaction (not *Pyrrhic*)

entries.related: *a Pyrrhic victory* — a win that costs so much it is almost a defeat; *an empty victory* — the same idea, less common; *a moral victory* — the reverse: a loss that still feels like a success.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: More than enough chances or time to do something.
entries.usage: Common in announcements, official statements and polite but firm emails, often to stress that someone had no excuse: *You had ample opportunity to object*. It usually has no article and is followed by *to* + verb or *for* + noun. *Ample* also goes with *time*, *evidence*, *space* and *parking*.
entries.pattern: have / give someone ample opportunity to + verb / for + noun
examples: There will be **ample opportunity** for questions after the presentation.
The landlord says we had **ample opportunity** to report the leak before it ruined the floor.
Our long layover in Lisbon gave us **ample opportunity** to explore the old town.

drill.sentence: During preseason, the coach gave the new players {{ample opportunity}} to prove themselves.
drill.hint: more than enough chances (a formal adjective, not *plenty of*)

entries.related: *plenty of opportunity* — the same, more casual; *every opportunity* — stresses that all possible chances were given; *a window of opportunity* — a short period when something is possible.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To give up your power over something or your responsibility for it, usually unwillingly.
entries.usage: Formal; common in business and political news (*relinquish control of the company*) and in talk about people who cannot let go, such as parents or founders. It often follows *refuse to*, *be reluctant to* or *be forced to*, with *of* or *over* + the thing. In conversation, *give up control* or *let go* is more natural.
entries.pattern: relinquish control of / over + company / project / territory
examples: The founder was forced to **relinquish control** of the company after the board voted him out.
Some parents find it hard to **relinquish control** when their kids leave for college.
The general promised to **relinquish control** to a civilian government within a year.

drill.sentence: After his stroke, my grandfather reluctantly agreed to {{relinquish control}} of the family farm to my aunt.
drill.hint: formally give up his power over it (not *give up* or *hand over*)

entries.related: *give up control* — plainer; *cede control* — formal, often of territory or power to another group; *hand over the reins* — informal, pass control to a successor.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To influence what people in general think about an issue, especially to move their view in one direction.
entries.usage: A news and politics phrase: campaigns, ads, trials, leaks and viral videos *sway public opinion*. It often follows *try to* or *help*, and the passive is common, as in *Public opinion was swayed by the photos*. *Shape public opinion* is broader and slower; *sway* suggests a push toward one side.
entries.pattern: sway public opinion (in favor of / against + noun)
examples: Both campaigns are spending millions on TV ads to **sway public opinion** before the vote.
A few viral videos of happy dogs helped **sway public opinion**, and the city decided to keep the dog park open.
The lawyers hoped the documentary would **sway public opinion** in their client's favor.

drill.sentence: Celebrity endorsements rarely {{sway public opinion}} on serious issues like taxes or school funding.
drill.hint: move what most people think toward one side (not *shift* or *shape*)

entries.related: *shape public opinion* — influence how it forms over time; *shift public opinion* — focuses on the change itself; *win over the public* — get people on your side.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Disagreements so deep that they cannot be resolved, especially between partners in a marriage.
entries.usage: It is the legal ground for a no-fault divorce in California and some other states, so Americans know it from celebrity divorce news. People also use it, often half-jokingly, for bands, business partners or roommates who split up. It is almost always plural, often after *cite* or *over*.
entries.pattern: cite irreconcilable differences; split over irreconcilable differences
examples: After twelve years of marriage, the couple filed for divorce, citing **irreconcilable differences**.
The band broke up in 2019 because of what the drummer called **irreconcilable differences** over money.
My roommate and I had **irreconcilable differences** about dirty dishes, so I moved out.

drill.sentence: When the singer and her husband announced their split, their joint statement cited {{irreconcilable differences}}.
drill.hint: disagreements that can never be settled (the standard divorce phrase)

entries.related: *creative differences* — the polite phrase when artists or bands split; *a falling-out* — a quarrel that ends a relationship; *irretrievable breakdown* — the legal wording used in some other places.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To think up a plan, usually in private and often with others, especially a clever, secret or mischievous one.
entries.usage: Common in storytelling, news and casual talk about surprise parties, pranks, schemes and crimes: *hatch a plan to …*. The tone can be playful (kids, friends) or suspicious (criminals, plotters), and *hatch a plot* or *hatch a scheme* work the same way. The passive is common, as in *The plan was hatched over dinner*.
entries.pattern: hatch a plan / plot / scheme to + verb
examples: Over coffee, my sisters and I **hatched a plan** to throw Mom a surprise party for her sixtieth.
Prosecutors say the two men **hatched the plan** while they were sharing a prison cell.
The **plan** to save the old movie theater **was hatched** at a neighborhood barbecue.

drill.sentence: While the teacher was out of the room, the students {{hatched a plan}} to hide her chair.
drill.hint: secretly thought up a scheme (the verb is also used for chicks and eggs)

entries.related: *come up with a plan* — neutral, no secrecy; *cook up* — informal, often a dishonest plan or excuse; *plot* — plan something harmful in secret.

entries.term: reserve the right to do something
entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To state that you keep the option to do something later if you decide to, so that nobody can claim you gave it up.
entries.usage: Standard wording in contracts, store policies, terms of service and official notices, as in *We reserve the right to refuse service*. In conversation it is used half-jokingly to keep an option open: *I reserve the right to change my mind*. It is followed by *to* + verb, and the subject is usually *we*, a company or *I*.
entries.pattern: reserve the right to + verb (refuse, cancel, change, edit)
examples: The hotel **reserves the right to** charge guests for any damage to the room.
I'll come to the party, but I **reserve the right to** leave early if I'm tired.
The newspaper **reserves the right to** edit letters for length and clarity.

drill.sentence: The sign by the door says the restaurant {{reserves the right to}} refuse service to anyone.
drill.hint: keeps the option to (the classic wording on store signs; not *has*)

entries.related: *retain the right to* — the same, rarer and more legal; *keep your options open* — informal, avoid committing; *waive the right to* — the opposite, formally give up a right.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To hurt someone who trusted you by doing something dishonest or disloyal, such as lying to them or sharing their secret.
entries.usage: A serious, emotional phrase about partners, friends, doctors, officials and companies. Common related forms are *feel betrayed* and the noun phrase *a betrayal of trust*. For smaller disappointments, *let someone down* is more natural.
entries.pattern: betray someone's trust; a betrayal of trust
examples: Her husband **betrayed her trust** by secretly emptying their joint savings account.
Voters feel the mayor **betrayed their trust** by hiding the city's debt.
A doctor who shares patient records without consent **betrays the trust** of the people he treats.

drill.sentence: My sister read my diary while I was at camp, and I felt she had completely {{betrayed my trust}}.
drill.hint: been disloyal to me after I had relied on her (not *broken*)

entries.related: *break someone's trust* — similar, a bit less dramatic; *abuse someone's trust* — use their trust for your own gain; *let someone down* — disappoint them, much milder.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To put someone's chances of success at risk by doing something that could make them fail.
entries.usage: Common in news, advice and serious conversation, often as a warning: *Don't do anything to jeopardize your chances*. Typical continuations are *of getting in*, *of winning*, *of a promotion* and *of recovery*. It is more formal than *hurt your chances*.
entries.pattern: jeopardize your / someone's chances of + -ing / noun
examples: One more late assignment could **jeopardize her chances** of getting into a good college.
The star player's knee injury may **jeopardize the team's chances** in the playoffs.
He didn't want to **jeopardize his chances** of a promotion by complaining too loudly.

drill.sentence: My doctor said that smoking after surgery could seriously {{jeopardize my chances}} of a full recovery.
drill.hint: put my prospects at risk (formal verb; not *hurt* or *ruin*)

entries.related: *hurt your chances* — plainer, more common in speech; *ruin your chances* — stronger, the chance is lost; *boost your chances* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: People who cannot easily leave or ignore what you say or show them, because of where they are.
entries.usage: Used about passengers, patients in waiting rooms, students and family at the dinner table, and about ads placed where people are stuck, such as on planes or at gas pumps. The tone is often critical or humorous: *have a captive audience*, *a captive audience for* + ads or opinions. It does not mean a fascinated audience; that is a *captivated* audience.
entries.pattern: have a captive audience; a captive audience for + ads / opinions
examples: Airlines know that passengers on a six-hour flight are **a captive audience** for their ads.
At family dinners, my uncle treats everyone at the table as **a captive audience** for his opinions.
Teachers have **a captive audience**, but that doesn't mean the students are listening.

drill.sentence: Stuck in the elevator for an hour, we became {{a captive audience}} for the man's endless stories about his cats.
drill.hint: listeners with no way to escape

entries.related: *a captivated audience* — fascinated, not trapped; *hold someone's attention* — keep them interested by choice; *preach to the choir* — talk to people who already agree.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A way of living that involves a lot of sitting and very little physical activity.
entries.usage: Common in health news and doctors' advice, usually as a risk: *a sedentary lifestyle raises the risk of …*. It sounds a bit clinical; in conversation people more often say *I sit all day*. The usual verb is *lead*, and *sedentary* also goes with *job*, *work* and *behavior*.
entries.pattern: lead a sedentary lifestyle; a sedentary job
examples: Doctors warn that **a sedentary lifestyle** can raise your risk of heart disease and diabetes.
Since I started working from home, I've slipped into **a sedentary lifestyle**, so I bought a standing desk.
Many city dogs lead **a sedentary lifestyle**, just like their owners.

drill.sentence: Long commutes and desk jobs mean that many Americans now lead {{a sedentary lifestyle}}.
drill.hint: a way of life with lots of sitting (formal adjective, not *inactive*)

entries.related: *an active lifestyle* — the opposite; *a couch potato* — informal, a person who sits and watches a lot of TV; *inactive* — the plainer adjective.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A very bad, painful headache, as if your head were breaking in two.
entries.usage: Very common in everyday conversation and writing, almost always after *have*, *get* or *wake up with*. In this sense *splitting* nearly always goes with *headache*; for other pain, say *severe*, *sharp* or *terrible*. It describes how the pain feels, so it is not the same as the medical term *migraine*.
entries.pattern: have / get / wake up with a splitting headache
examples: I woke up with **a splitting headache** after only four hours of sleep.
Six hours of staring at spreadsheets gave me **a splitting headache**.
She skipped the concert because she had **a splitting headache** and couldn't stand bright lights.

drill.sentence: Could you turn down the TV, please? I've got {{a splitting headache}}.
drill.hint: head pain so bad your skull feels like it's breaking in two

entries.related: *a pounding headache* — with a beating rhythm; *a migraine* — a specific medical condition, not just a bad headache; *a dull headache* — mild but steady.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Someone who wakes up easily, for example because of small noises or light.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, especially when explaining your needs to a partner, roommate, host or hotel: *I'm a light sleeper*. It describes the person, so it follows *be*; the verb form is *sleep lightly*. The opposite is *a heavy sleeper* or *a deep sleeper*.
entries.pattern: be a light sleeper (opposite: a heavy / deep sleeper)
examples: I'm **a light sleeper**, so even the refrigerator humming can wake me up.
When you book the hotel, ask for a quiet room; my husband is **a very light sleeper**.
Our newborn is **a light sleeper**, so we tiptoe around the apartment after eight.

drill.sentence: Please don't run the dishwasher at night. My roommate is {{a light sleeper}}, and the noise bothers her.
drill.hint: someone who wakes up very easily

mistake.wrong: I have a very light sleep, so I need earplugs.
mistake.right: I'm a very light sleeper, so I need earplugs.
mistake.why: Many languages say "have a light sleep," but English describes the person: *be a light sleeper* or *sleep lightly*.

entries.related: *a heavy sleeper* or *a deep sleeper* — the opposite, hard to wake; *a night owl* — someone who stays up late; *toss and turn* — move around in bed because you cannot sleep.

entries.label: noun + noun
entries.meaning: The things that make life physically comfortable, such as good food, warmth, a soft bed and hot water.
entries.usage: Almost always plural and common when people talk about camping, travel, moving or living simply: *miss your creature comforts*, *all the creature comforts of home*. The tone is light and a little humorous. It means everyday comforts and conveniences, not luxury or emotional comfort.
entries.pattern: miss / enjoy (all) the creature comforts (of home)
examples: After two weeks of camping, I really missed my **creature comforts**, like a hot shower and a real bed.
The cabin is tiny, but it has all the **creature comforts**: Wi-Fi, a coffee maker and heated floors.
Even on a tight budget, most students won't give up **creature comforts** like streaming services and takeout.

drill.sentence: The hostel was cheap and clean, but it lacked basic {{creature comforts}} like towels and hot water.
drill.hint: things that make daily life physically pleasant (two words, not *amenities*)

entries.related: *home comforts* — the same idea, more common in British English; *amenities* — useful features of a hotel or building, more formal; *the finer things in life* — luxury, not basic comfort.

entries.label: adverb + verb
entries.meaning: To reduce something by a very large amount, usually through strong or sudden action.
entries.usage: Common in news, business, health and policy talk: *drastically reduce costs, emissions, waiting times, the risk of …*. *Drastically* suggests a big and sometimes painful change, so it can sound alarming when the cuts are to services. The adverb usually goes before the verb; in speech it can also follow the object, as in *reduce costs drastically*.
entries.pattern: drastically reduce + costs / emissions / the risk of …
examples: Switching to LED bulbs **drastically reduced** our electricity bill.
Better car seats have **drastically reduced** the number of young children hurt in crashes.
Budget cuts forced the library to **drastically reduce** its opening hours.

drill.sentence: If you want to {{drastically reduce}} your sugar intake, start by cutting out soda.
drill.hint: cut by a huge amount, with strong action (not *dramatically*)

entries.related: *dramatically reduce* — similar, stresses how striking the change is; *slash* — informal, cut sharply, especially prices or budgets; *gradually reduce* — the opposite, step by step.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A job with no chance of promotion or progress, which leads nowhere in your career.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and journalism, and it sounds critical or self-pitying: *stuck in a dead-end job*. It usually suggests low pay and no future, not necessarily a bad workplace. Use a hyphen before a noun (*a dead-end job*) but not in the noun form (*the job is a dead end*).
entries.pattern: be stuck in / quit / leave a dead-end job
examples: He spent five years in **a dead-end job** at a warehouse before going back to school.
Many young people feel trapped in **dead-end jobs** with no health insurance.
Don't stay in **a dead-end job** just because the commute is short.

drill.sentence: She was tired of answering phones in {{a dead-end job}}, so she started taking night classes in nursing.
drill.hint: work with no future and no chance of promotion

entries.related: *a stepping stone* — the opposite, a job that leads to better ones; *a career ladder* — the path of promotions this kind of job lacks; *a rut* — a boring routine that is hard to escape.

entries.label: noun + noun
entries.meaning: The smallest number of staff needed to keep a business, office or service running, for example during holidays or a strike.
entries.usage: Common in news and workplace talk about holidays, night shifts, strikes and government shutdowns: *run on a skeleton crew*, *operate with a skeleton crew*. It often explains why service is slow or limited. *Skeleton staff* means the same and is more common in British English.
entries.pattern: run on / operate with a skeleton crew
examples: Between Christmas and New Year's, the office runs on **a skeleton crew**.
During the government shutdown, national parks stayed open with only **a skeleton crew** of rangers.
The restaurant was down to **a skeleton crew**, so we waited an hour for our food.

drill.sentence: Our local post office stays open the day after Thanksgiving, but only with {{a skeleton crew}}.
drill.hint: the bare minimum of workers (not *… staff*)

entries.related: *skeleton staff* — the same idea, more common in British English; *short-staffed* — having fewer workers than needed; *a full crew* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To become calm and in control of yourself again after being upset, shocked or very emotional.
entries.usage: Common in storytelling, news and sports reports, often about someone who cried, laughed or panicked in public: *She paused to regain her composure*. The possessive matches the subject (*he regained his composure*). In casual speech, *pull yourself together* is more common.
entries.pattern: pause / take a moment to regain your composure
examples: The witness broke down in tears and needed a minute to **regain her composure**.
After a shaky first inning, the young pitcher **regained his composure** and struck out the next three batters.
When the doctor called with my test results, it took me a moment to **regain my composure**.

drill.sentence: The groom's voice cracked during his speech, but he took a deep breath and {{regained his composure}}.
drill.hint: became calm and in control again (not *recovered*)

entries.related: *lose your composure* — the opposite; *pull yourself together* — informal, often said as advice; *keep your cool* — stay calm, without losing it first.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A strong, widespread protest by ordinary people against a decision, event or injustice.
entries.usage: A news and politics phrase: *spark*, *cause* or *provoke a public outcry*, often followed by *over* or *against*. It implies that the protest is loud and broad, and it often forces officials or companies to change course. It is also used without *a*, as in *after public outcry*.
entries.pattern: spark / cause / provoke a public outcry (over + noun)
examples: The plan to close the children's hospital sparked **a public outcry**, and the governor reversed it within a week.
After **a public outcry** over ticket prices, the band added cheaper seats.
The brand pulled the ad following **public outcry** on social media.

drill.sentence: The decision to cut half the city's bus routes led to {{a public outcry}}, and the council voted to restore them.
drill.hint: a wave of loud protest from ordinary people (not *outrage*)

entries.related: *outrage* — strong anger, not always expressed as protest; *backlash* — a strong negative reaction, often against a change; *uproar* — loud, confused public anger.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To make someone feel more confident, especially when their confidence is weak or needs support.
entries.usage: Common in sports, education, business and news; typical subjects are wins, praise, good results and good news. It sounds a little more formal than *boost* and suggests support for something that might otherwise weaken. *Bolster confidence in* + noun is used for the economy, a system or a leader.
entries.pattern: bolster someone's confidence; bolster confidence in + noun
examples: Winning their first game of the season really **bolstered the kids' confidence**.
Practicing in front of a few friends can **bolster your confidence** before an audition.
The strong jobs report helped **bolster confidence** in the economy.

drill.sentence: Learning to drive at sixty really {{bolstered her confidence}}, and now she travels on her own.
drill.hint: made her feel more sure of herself (formal verb, not *boosted*)

entries.related: *boost someone's confidence* — the same, more common in speech; *shake someone's confidence* — the opposite; *reassure* — make someone less worried.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Damage so serious that it cannot be repaired or undone.
entries.usage: Used in news, law, medicine and serious conversation about health, buildings, nature, reputations and relationships: *cause* or *do irreparable damage to*. *Damage* is uncountable here, so there is no *a* or *an*. Stress the second syllable of *irreparable* (ih-REP-er-uh-bul), not *pair*.
entries.pattern: cause / do / suffer irreparable damage (to + noun)
examples: The fire did **irreparable damage** to the church's two-hundred-year-old paintings.
Some friendships suffer **irreparable damage** over a single careless comment.
Left untreated, glaucoma can cause **irreparable damage** to the optic nerve.

drill.sentence: Washing the antique quilt in hot water caused {{irreparable damage}}; the colors ran and the fabric tore.
drill.hint: harm that can never be fixed (not *permanent* or *irreversible*)

mistake.wrong: The flood caused an irreparable damage to the house.
mistake.right: The flood caused irreparable damage to the house.
mistake.why: *Damage* is uncountable in this sense, so it takes no *a* or *an*; the plural *damages* means money paid after a lawsuit.

entries.related: *irreversible damage* — cannot be undone, common about health and the environment; *lasting damage* — continues for a long time; *beyond repair* — the same idea, placed after the noun.

entries.label: verb + adverb
entries.meaning: To take action quickly and decisively, especially in response to a problem or an emergency.
entries.usage: Typical of news, official statements and leadership talk: governments, police, banks and companies *act swiftly to* + verb. *Swiftly* is more formal than *quickly* and suggests effective, decisive action. It often follows *must*, *need to* or *promise to*.
entries.pattern: act swiftly (to + verb: contain, stop, fix)
examples: The bank **acted swiftly** to block my card after someone used it in another country.
The governor promised to **act swiftly** to help families who lost their homes in the flood.
If you notice the signs of a stroke, **act swiftly** and call nine-one-one.

drill.sentence: Firefighters {{acted swiftly}} to stop the blaze from spreading to the nearby houses.
drill.hint: took fast, decisive action (formal adverb, not *quickly*)

entries.related: *act quickly* — neutral, more common in speech; *act decisively* — stresses firmness more than speed; *drag your feet* — the opposite, delay on purpose.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A project that someone cares about personally and gives special attention to, often more than others think it deserves.
entries.usage: Common in politics, business and family life: a mayor's, a CEO's or a parent's *pet project*. The tone can be neutral or slightly critical, suggesting favoritism or wasted money. *Pet* has the same sense in *pet peeve*, *pet theory* and *pet cause*.
entries.pattern: someone's pet project
examples: The new bike lanes were the mayor's **pet project**, and she fought hard to fund them.
Restoring the old Mustang has been my dad's **pet project** since he retired.
The company spent millions on the CEO's **pet project**, a smart fridge that nobody bought.

drill.sentence: The community garden started as my neighbor's {{pet project}}, but now half the block helps out.
drill.hint: an undertaking someone personally loves and pushes (not *passion …*)

entries.related: *a passion project* — work done for love rather than money, more positive; *a labor of love* — hard work done for pleasure; *a pet peeve* — a small thing that always annoys you.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To tell someone, in a polite and somewhat formal way, that you are sorry about the death of someone close to them.
entries.usage: Used in speech, cards, emails and official statements: *I'd like to offer my condolences*, *offer condolences to the family*. *Condolences* is almost always plural in this phrase. In casual speech, *I'm so sorry for your loss* is more common.
entries.pattern: offer your condolences (to someone)
examples: We went to the funeral home to **offer our condolences** to his widow.
The president called the families of the victims to **offer his condolences**.
I just heard about your grandmother, and I wanted to **offer my condolences**.

drill.sentence: When our neighbor's husband died, we brought her a casserole and {{offered our condolences}}.
drill.hint: told her formally how sorry we were (not *sympathy*)

entries.related: *express your sympathy* — similar, a little less formal; *pay your respects* — visit or attend a funeral to honor the person who died; *I'm sorry for your loss* — the most common spoken form.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To stop yourself from showing how excited you are, usually with difficulty.
entries.usage: Mostly used with *can barely*, *could hardly* or *try to*: *She could barely contain her excitement*. Said sarcastically, *Try to contain your excitement* mocks someone who is clearly bored. *Contain* works the same way with *anger*, *joy* and *laughter*.
entries.pattern: can barely / could hardly contain your excitement
examples: The kids could barely **contain their excitement** on the drive to Disneyland.
"We're doing inventory all weekend. Try to **contain your excitement**," my manager said dryly.
She tried to **contain her excitement** during the interview, but she was grinning when she walked out.

drill.sentence: When the letter from Juilliard arrived, my sister could hardly {{contain her excitement}}.
drill.hint: keep her thrill from showing (not *hide*)

entries.related: *contain yourself* — the same idea without the noun; *hide your excitement* — similar, stresses keeping it secret; *be beside yourself* — so emotional that you lose control.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: The usual price or pay for something at the moment, according to the market.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and business about wages, fees, rents and prices, often in the question *What's the going rate for …?* It is almost always used with *the*. It refers to a market norm, not an official price, so people use it to judge whether an offer is fair.
entries.pattern: the going rate for + service / job
examples: Do you know **the going rate** for a babysitter in this neighborhood?
Freelance translators often charge below **the going rate** just to get their first clients.
In some cities, five thousand dollars a month is now **the going rate** for a two-bedroom apartment.

drill.sentence: My plumber charged me double {{the going rate}}, and I didn't realize it until a friend told me.
drill.hint: the normal price at the moment (not *market* or *usual*)

entries.related: *the market rate* — the same idea, more technical; *the asking price* — what a seller wants, which may be higher; *a rip-off* — informal, a price that is much too high.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To show through your words or behavior that you feel sorry and guilty for something wrong you did.
entries.usage: Common in court reporting, news and serious talk about crimes and scandals, where judges and the public watch whether someone *shows remorse*. It is very often negative: *show no remorse*, *show little remorse*. *Remorse* is uncountable and deeper than *regret*, because it involves moral guilt.
entries.pattern: show (no / little / genuine) remorse (for + noun)
examples: The judge gave him the maximum sentence because he **showed no remorse** for the attack.
The player later **showed remorse** for the hard foul and called the injured opponent to apologize.
Fans might forgive the quarterback if he **showed real remorse** instead of blaming his teammates.

drill.sentence: My little brother broke my phone and {{showed no remorse}}; he just shrugged and went back to his game.
drill.hint: gave no sign that he felt sorry

entries.related: *regret* — sorry about a past choice, not necessarily a moral wrong; *contrition* — formal, sincere sorrow and a wish to make up for it; *remorseless* — showing no remorse.

entries.label: verb + adverb
entries.meaning: To grow faster and faster, so that the amount increases at an ever-increasing rate.
entries.usage: Common in science, finance and news, and in casual speech as an exaggeration for *very fast*. Strictly, *exponential* growth means the amount multiplies by the same factor in each period, as with compound interest or an epidemic. Careful writers avoid it for growth that is merely large.
entries.pattern: grow / increase / rise exponentially
examples: After two dozen rabbits were released in Australia in 1859, their numbers **grew exponentially**.
Thanks to compound interest, your savings **grow exponentially** the longer you leave them alone.
Since her video went viral, orders for her handmade candles have **grown exponentially**.

drill.sentence: If each person tells two friends, and each of them tells two more, the number of people who know will {{grow exponentially}}.
drill.hint: get bigger at a faster and faster rate (not *increase*)

entries.related: *grow rapidly* — fast, without the mathematical sense; *snowball* — informal, grow faster and faster; *grow linearly* — by the same amount in each period.

entries.label: verb + adverb
entries.meaning: To differ a lot from one case, place or person to another.
entries.usage: Common in news, reports, health advice and explanations, often about prices, rules, results or opinions: *Prices vary widely depending on …*. The subject is usually plural or uncountable (*costs*, *opinions*, *quality*). *Vary greatly* and *vary considerably* mean the same; *vary wildly* is stronger and more informal.
entries.pattern: X varies widely (from … to … / depending on …)
examples: Rents **vary widely** across the city, from twelve hundred to over four thousand dollars a month.
Flu symptoms can **vary widely** from one person to another.
Opinions in my family **vary widely** on whether pineapple belongs on pizza.

drill.sentence: Laws on fireworks {{vary widely}} from state to state, so check before the Fourth of July.
drill.hint: differ a lot (not *greatly* or *wildly*)

entries.related: *vary considerably* — more formal; *range from … to …* — names the limits; *be uniform* — the opposite, the same everywhere.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A period in the past that has ended and whose way of life no longer exists.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, travel writing and nostalgic talk: *a relic of a bygone era*, *a reminder of a bygone era*. It sounds a little literary and often nostalgic, sometimes ironic. *Bygone* is used almost only before a noun (*bygone days*, *a bygone age*).
entries.pattern: a relic / reminder of a bygone era
examples: With its jukebox and red leather booths, the diner feels like a relic of **a bygone era**.
To my kids, handwritten letters seem like something from **a bygone era**.
Full-service gas stations, where someone washes your windshield, seem to belong to **a bygone era**.

drill.sentence: Grandpa still wears a hat and tie to the grocery store, like a gentleman from {{a bygone era}}.
drill.hint: a long-gone period (literary adjective, not *another*)

entries.related: *the good old days* — informal and nostalgic; *a thing of the past* — something that no longer exists; *yesteryear* — a literary word for the past.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To have a sudden, uncontrolled fit of anger, like a small child who screams, cries or kicks.
entries.usage: Used literally for toddlers and, critically or humorously, for adults who behave childishly, such as athletes, celebrities or bosses. *Have a tantrum* is also common, and *temper tantrum* is the full form. In American English, *throw a fit* means much the same.
entries.pattern: throw a (temper) tantrum (over / about + noun)
examples: My two-year-old **threw a tantrum** in the middle of the grocery store because I wouldn't buy candy.
The tennis player **threw a tantrum** and smashed his racket after a bad line call.
When the restaurant ran out of steak, a customer **threw a full-blown tantrum** at the host stand.

drill.sentence: When his flight was canceled, a grown man {{threw a tantrum}} at the gate, yelling and kicking his suitcase.
drill.hint: had a childish outburst of anger (not *a fit*)

entries.related: *throw a fit* — very similar, common in the US; *have a meltdown* — informal, lose control under stress; *sulk* — be quietly angry and silent.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To deliberately start an argument or a fight with someone.
entries.usage: Used in conversation and news about people, countries and companies: *pick a fight with someone*, often *over* + topic. The tone is critical, because the person who picks the fight is the aggressor. It often follows *try to* or *be looking to*, as in *He was just looking to pick a fight*.
entries.pattern: pick a fight (with someone) (over + noun)
examples: He'd had a few drinks and was **picking fights** with everyone at the bar.
Please don't **pick a fight** with your brother right before we leave for Grandma's.
Critics say the airline is **picking a fight** with its pilots' union to avoid giving raises.

drill.sentence: I'm too tired to argue tonight, so if you're trying to {{pick a fight}}, I'm going to bed.
drill.hint: deliberately start an argument (the verb is not *start*)

entries.related: *start an argument* — neutral, not always on purpose; *pick a quarrel* — older and more formal; *be spoiling for a fight* — be eager to fight.

entries.label: adverb + verb
entries.meaning: To pretend to forget something, or fail to mention it, because remembering it would not suit you.
entries.usage: An ironic, critical phrase used in conversation, opinion pieces and politics. *Conveniently* here means "in a way that happens to suit them," so it accuses the person of being dishonest or selective. It often appears as *conveniently forget to mention that …*.
entries.pattern: conveniently forget (to mention) + something / that …
examples: My teenage son always **conveniently forgets** that it's his turn to take out the trash.
The seller **conveniently forgot** to mention that the basement floods every spring.
When he tells the story, my dad **conveniently forgets** that he was the one who got us lost.

drill.sentence: Every time the check arrives, my uncle {{conveniently forgets}} his wallet.
drill.hint: leaves behind on purpose and pretends it was an accident (ironic adverb + verb)

entries.related: *selective memory* — remembering only what suits you; *turn a blind eye* — ignore something on purpose; *gloss over* — mention a problem only briefly to hide it.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Frustration that has built up inside someone over a long time without being expressed.
entries.usage: Used in conversation, journalism and psychology, often when the feeling finally comes out: *release*, *vent* or *let out pent-up frustration*. *Pent-up* also goes with *anger*, *energy* and *emotions*, and in economics with *demand*. It takes a hyphen before a noun.
entries.pattern: release / vent / let out (your) pent-up frustration
examples: Years of **pent-up frustration** came out when she finally told her boss what she thought of him.
Some people go to boxing classes after work to let out their **pent-up frustration**.
The protests reflect **pent-up frustration** over rising rents and stagnant wages.

drill.sentence: After an hour stuck in traffic, he slammed the car door, letting out all his {{pent-up frustration}}.
drill.hint: annoyance that had been building inside him (hyphenated adjective, not *bottled-up*)

entries.related: *bottled-up* — similar, stresses keeping feelings hidden; *vent* — express strong feelings, often to someone; *pent-up demand* — economics, demand that is waiting to be met.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Hurt pride after a failure, rejection or criticism, when nothing more serious than your self-image is damaged.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, sports writing and news, and often light or humorous: *nurse a bruised ego*, *leave with a bruised ego*. It suggests the hurt is real but small and temporary. For a deeper hurt, *wounded pride* fits better.
entries.pattern: nurse / leave with / escape with a bruised ego
examples: He fell off his skateboard in front of the whole school but escaped with nothing worse than **a bruised ego**.
After losing a chess match to a ten-year-old, I went home to nurse **a bruised ego**.
Getting rejected by three publishers left her with **a bruised ego**, but she kept writing.

drill.sentence: When his younger brother beat him at basketball, he spent the evening in his room nursing {{a bruised ego}}.
drill.hint: hurt pride (adjective + noun, not *wounded pride*)

entries.related: *wounded pride* — similar, a bit more serious; *swallow your pride* — accept something that hurts your pride; *massage someone's ego* — flatter them.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A past that includes some bad, dishonest or embarrassing episodes, such as failures, scandals or crimes.
entries.usage: Used in journalism, biographies and conversation about people, companies and places: *a man with a checkered past*. It hints at trouble without details, so it is softer than *a criminal record* and can sound slightly amused. British English uses the same phrase but spells it *chequered*.
entries.pattern: have a checkered past; someone with a checkered past
examples: The new treasurer has **a checkered past**, including two bankruptcies and a fraud investigation.
Despite her **checkered past**, the singer is now one of the most respected voices in country music.
Tour guides love to tell visitors about the old hotel's **checkered past**.

drill.sentence: Before you hire that contractor, look him up online; I've heard he has {{a checkered past}}.
drill.hint: a history that includes some dishonest episodes (not *shady* or *dark*)

entries.related: *a shady past* — more clearly dishonest; *a skeleton in the closet* — one hidden, shameful secret; *a clean record* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To speak publicly about something after saying nothing about it for a long time.
entries.usage: A typical news headline phrase: celebrities, officials and victims *break their silence on* or *about* a scandal, a breakup or an accusation. It suggests that the silence was noticed, so the statement matters. In everyday speech it is often used jokingly.
entries.pattern: break your silence on / about + topic
examples: After months of rumors, the singer finally **broke her silence** about the divorce in a TV interview.
The company's CEO waited two weeks before he **broke his silence** on the data leak.
After a month off social media, my brother **broke his silence** with a photo of his new puppy.

drill.sentence: The family of the missing hiker {{broke their silence}} today, thanking volunteers for their help.
drill.hint: spoke publicly for the first time after saying nothing

entries.related: *speak out* — speak publicly, usually against something; *open up about* — talk about private feelings; *remain silent* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: An extremely distressing and frightening experience that leaves people shaken.
entries.usage: Common in news reports, survivor stories and serious conversation about accidents, disasters, crimes or medical emergencies. *Harrowing* is strong, so using it for small problems sounds exaggerated or humorous. It also goes with *ordeal*, *account*, *journey* and *story*.
entries.pattern: a harrowing experience / ordeal / account (of …)
examples: The family spent two days trapped in their car during the blizzard, **a harrowing experience** none of them will forget.
Passengers described the emergency landing as **a harrowing experience**.
Anyone who has assembled IKEA furniture with a spouse knows what **a harrowing experience** it can be.

drill.sentence: Being robbed at gunpoint was {{a harrowing experience}}, and she still has nightmares about it.
drill.hint: deeply distressing and frightening (not *horrifying* or *traumatic*)

entries.related: *traumatic* — causing lasting psychological harm; *an ordeal* — a long, painful experience; *nerve-racking* — making you very nervous, much milder.

entries.label: verb + prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: To act honestly and with good intentions, without trying to deceive or cheat anyone.
entries.usage: Common in law, business, negotiations and political debate; related forms are *negotiate in good faith* and *a good-faith effort*. Saying someone did not act in good faith is a serious accusation, and the opposite is *in bad faith*. Before a noun it is hyphenated: *a good-faith offer*.
entries.pattern: act / negotiate in good faith; a good-faith effort
examples: The landlord **acted in good faith**; he honestly didn't know the heater was broken.
I know you **acted in good faith**, but next time please check with me before you sign anything.
The court ruled that the buyer had **acted in good faith** and could keep the painting.

drill.sentence: The referee made a bad call, but he {{acted in good faith}}; he really believed the ball was out.
drill.hint: behaved honestly, with no intent to deceive (fixed phrase)

entries.related: *in bad faith* — dishonestly, intending to deceive; *mean well* — informal, have good intentions; *a good-faith effort* — a sincere attempt.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: An extremely small difference between winning and losing, especially in an election or a vote.
entries.usage: A favorite of American political journalism: *win by a razor-thin margin*, *a razor-thin majority*. It also appears in sports and in business, where *razor-thin profit margins* means almost no profit. British English more often says *wafer-thin*.
entries.pattern: win / lose / pass by a razor-thin margin
examples: The senator won reelection by **a razor-thin margin** of just four hundred votes.
Grocery stores operate on **razor-thin margins**, so a small rise in costs can wipe out their profit.
The race was decided by **a razor-thin margin**, with the winner ahead by a hundredth of a second.

drill.sentence: The vote on the new school budget passed by {{a razor-thin margin}}, fifty-one to forty-nine percent.
drill.hint: an extremely small difference (hyphenated adjective, not *slim* or *narrow*)

entries.related: *a narrow margin* — neutral, small but not extreme; *wafer-thin* — the same idea, more British; *a landslide* — the opposite, a huge win.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Problems or questions that have not been resolved yet and still need attention.
entries.usage: Common in work emails, meetings, negotiations and news about deals: *resolve the outstanding issues*, *a few outstanding issues remain*. Here *outstanding* means "still open," not "excellent," so context matters. The same sense appears in *outstanding bills*, *an outstanding balance* and *outstanding questions*.
entries.pattern: resolve / address the outstanding issues; a few outstanding issues remain
examples: Before we sign the lease, there are two **outstanding issues**: the parking space and the pet deposit.
Negotiators say a trade deal is close, but several **outstanding issues** remain.
Let's go through any **outstanding issues** at the end of the call.

drill.sentence: The sale of the house is almost done; the only {{outstanding issue}} is who pays for the new roof.
drill.hint: unresolved matter (the adjective can also mean *excellent*)

entries.related: *unresolved issues* — the same, also used for emotional problems; *loose ends* — small unfinished details, informal; *open questions* — things not yet decided.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To find the exact reason for a problem or event, not just a general idea of it.
entries.usage: Common in medicine, accident reports, repairs and everyday troubleshooting: *pinpoint the cause of the pain, the fire, the delay*. It often follows *hard to*, *try to* or *can't*, because the cause is not obvious. Adding *exact* (*pinpoint the exact cause*) stresses precision even more.
entries.pattern: pinpoint the (exact) cause of + problem
examples: It took the mechanic three days to **pinpoint the cause** of the strange noise in my engine.
Fire officials haven't been able to **pinpoint the cause**, but they suspect faulty wiring.
**Pinpointing the cause** of chronic back pain is often harder than treating it.

drill.sentence: The plumber spent all morning trying to {{pinpoint the cause}} of the leak behind the kitchen wall.
drill.hint: find the exact reason (not *identify* or *track down*)

entries.related: *identify the cause* — more neutral, less stress on precision; *get to the bottom of* — informal, find the real explanation; *the root cause* — the deepest, original cause.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To become responsible for paying costs because of something you do or something that happens.
entries.usage: Formal and typical of contracts, insurance, business and financial writing; *incur* also goes with *fees*, *charges*, *expenses*, *debt* and *losses*. The costs are usually unwanted or a side effect, and the past participle after the noun is common: *costs incurred during the move*. In conversation, people usually say *end up paying* instead.
entries.pattern: incur (additional / significant) costs / fees / charges
examples: The city **incurred huge costs** cleaning up after the hurricane.
You won't **incur any costs** for returning the item within thirty days.
Any **costs incurred** during the move will be paid by the company.

drill.sentence: If you break the lease early, you could {{incur costs}} of up to three months' rent.
drill.hint: become responsible for paying (formal verb, not *face*)

mistake.wrong: Please send us a list of all occurred costs.
mistake.right: Please send us a list of all costs incurred.
mistake.why: *Occur* means "happen" and takes no object; costs that someone must pay are *incurred*.

entries.related: *run up* — informal, let debts or bills grow; *bear the cost* — pay a cost that falls on you; *absorb costs* — pay them yourself instead of passing them on.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Boring, low-status jobs that need little skill or thought, such as cleaning, sorting or carrying things.
entries.usage: Common in workplace talk, journalism and discussions of automation and low-wage work: *do*, *handle* or *be stuck with menial tasks*. It suggests the work is beneath someone's skills, so it can sound dismissive about other people's jobs. *Menial* also goes with *work*, *labor* and *jobs*.
entries.pattern: do / handle / be stuck with menial tasks
examples: As an intern, I spent most of my summer doing **menial tasks** like making copies and fetching coffee.
Robots at the distribution center now handle many **menial tasks**, such as moving boxes between shelves.
She hired a teenager to help with **menial tasks** around the house, like raking leaves.

drill.sentence: As a new nurse, she didn't mind the {{menial tasks}}, like restocking supplies and changing sheets.
drill.hint: low-status jobs that need little skill (not *mundane*)

entries.related: *mundane tasks* — dull and ordinary, without the low-status idea; *grunt work* — informal, the hard, boring part of a job; *drudgery* — hard, boring work.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A job or role that is hard and necessary but brings no thanks, praise or reward.
entries.usage: Used in conversation and journalism about referees, parents, volunteers, moderators and anyone who organizes things for others: *It's a thankless job, but someone has to do it*. It sounds sympathetic toward the person doing it. *A thankless task* means the same.
entries.pattern: a thankless job / task (but someone has to do it)
examples: Refereeing kids' soccer is **a thankless job**; parents yell at you no matter what you call.
My mom has done **the thankless job** of organizing the family reunion for twenty years.
Content moderators do **a thankless job**, reviewing disturbing posts so the rest of us never see them.

drill.sentence: Planning the office holiday party is {{a thankless job}}: if it goes well, nobody notices, and if it doesn't, everyone complains.
drill.hint: hard work that nobody appreciates (adjective, not *tough*)

entries.related: *an uphill battle* — a long struggle against difficulties; *an unsung hero* — someone whose important work gets no praise; *a labor of love* — hard work done gladly for its own sake.

entries.label: fixed phrase
entries.meaning: A time in the future that is fairly soon, though the exact time is not known.
entries.usage: Common in news, speeches, business and science writing, almost always as *in the not-too-distant future*. It is softer and vaguer than *soon* and sounds a little formal or dramatic, so it often introduces predictions. *The near future* means about the same and is more common.
entries.pattern: in the not-too-distant future
examples: We hope to move to a bigger house in **the not-too-distant future**.
In **the not-too-distant future**, self-driving taxis could be common in most big cities.
Experts warn that the reservoir could run dry in **the not-too-distant future** if the drought continues.

drill.sentence: My parents are planning to retire to Arizona in {{the not-too-distant future}}, probably in three or four years.
drill.hint: fairly soon, though not exactly when (not *the near …*)

entries.related: *the near future* — the same, more common; *down the road* — informal, at some point later; *in the long run* — over a long period.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To pay attention to a warning and act on it.
entries.usage: Formal and common in news about disasters, health and politics, very often in the negative: *failed to heed the warnings*. In conversation *heed* sounds literary, so people say *listen to* or *take a warning seriously*. *Heed* also goes with *advice* and *a call*.
entries.pattern: heed a / the warning(s); fail to heed …
examples: Residents who **heeded the warnings** and left before the hurricane were safe.
I wish I'd **heeded the warning** on the label; the hot sauce really was extremely hot.
Economists say the government failed to **heed warnings** about the housing bubble.

drill.sentence: Swimmers who don't {{heed the warnings}} about rip currents put the lifeguards' lives at risk too.
drill.hint: pay attention to the alerts and act on them (formal one-syllable verb)

entries.related: *ignore a warning* — the opposite; *take a warning seriously* — common in conversation; *a cautionary tale* — a story that serves as a warning.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To try every possible way of solving a problem, so that nothing is left to try.
entries.usage: Common in serious conversation, news, law and medicine, usually before a last step: *Once we've exhausted all options, we'll …*. The perfect and the passive are typical: *All other options have been exhausted*. *Exhaust all avenues* and *exhaust all possibilities* are close variants.
entries.pattern: exhaust all (other) options / avenues (before + -ing)
examples: We **exhausted all options** for saving the old oak tree before we finally had it cut down.
Doctors only recommend surgery once all other **options have been exhausted**.
Before you take out a payday loan, make sure you've **exhausted all your options**.

drill.sentence: We only called a locksmith after we'd {{exhausted all options}}: credit cards, a coat hanger, even the dog door.
drill.hint: tried every possible method (verb meaning *use up completely*)

entries.related: *run out of options* — have no choices left, more passive; *leave no stone unturned* — search or try everywhere; *a last resort* — what you do when every other option has failed.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To criticize or judge someone's behavior or character, often without knowing the full story or having the right to.
entries.usage: Usually used in the negative or in challenges, as in *I'm not passing judgment* or *Who are you to pass judgment on her?* It suggests moral superiority, so it is mostly used to criticize the person who judges. In a court, a judge *passes judgment* in the literal sense.
entries.pattern: pass judgment on + someone / someone's choices
examples: It's easy to **pass judgment on** other parents until you have a screaming toddler of your own.
The documentary shows the family's struggle without **passing judgment**.
Who are you to **pass judgment on** my lifestyle when you've never even met my friends?

drill.sentence: I don't want to {{pass judgment on}} my neighbors, but leaving their dog outside all night in January seems cruel.
drill.hint: act as a moral critic of (not just *judge*)

entries.related: *judge* — the plain verb; *be judgmental* — tend to criticize others; *give someone the benefit of the doubt* — the opposite attitude.
